name: Encryption
intent: Scramble data with a key so that only people holding the key can read it or change it, whether it is crossing a network, sitting on a disk or never leaving the user's device.
scenario: A notes app stores users' private notes. Attackers might sniff the network, steal a backup, break into the server or bribe a database administrator. Which of them can read a note depends on where the data is encrypted and who holds the keys.
problem: Access controls only help while the software enforcing them is intact. Data that is copied, stolen or read below the application is unprotected unless the bytes themselves are unreadable. But encryption is only as good as its key management, and it protects against different attackers depending on where it is applied.

howItWorks.title: Symmetric encryption: one key locks and unlocks
howItWorks.text: Algorithms such as AES-256 use the same secret key to encrypt (turn readable data into unreadable ciphertext) and decrypt. They are fast and used for bulk data. The challenge is getting the key to both sides safely.

howItWorks.title: Asymmetric encryption: a public key and a private key
howItWorks.text: With a key pair, anyone can encrypt with the public key but only the holder of the private key can decrypt (and the reverse is used for signatures). It solves key distribution but is slower, so it is typically used to agree on or protect a symmetric key (this is how TLS works).

howItWorks.title: Use authenticated encryption
howItWorks.text: Modes such as AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 add an authentication tag, so any modification of the ciphertext is detected on decryption. Encryption alone hides data but does not stop it being changed. Each encryption needs a unique nonce (a number used once) for the same key, because reusing one breaks the security.

howItWorks.title: Choose where to encrypt: in transit, at rest, end to end
howItWorks.text: In transit (TLS) protects the network path. At rest (disk, database or backup encryption) protects stolen storage. End-to-end means only the users hold the keys, so even the service operator cannot read the data. Each protects against a different attacker, and each moves the problem to protecting a key.

howItWorks.title: Manage the keys, because that is the real difficulty
howItWorks.text: Never store the key beside the data it protects. Keep keys in a key management service or hardware module, use envelope encryption (a data key encrypts the data, a master key encrypts the data key), rotate keys, and limit and log who can use them. A lost key means lost data.

pros: Stolen disks, backups and network captures are useless without the key
Reduces the damage of many kinds of breach
Standard algorithms are fast and widely available
End-to-end encryption limits what even the operator can access
cons: Key management is hard, and a lost key means lost data
Encrypted data is harder to search, sort and process on the server
Does not help once data is decrypted in a compromised running application
Misuse (reused nonces, homemade schemes, weak modes) can make it worthless
whenToUse: In transit for all traffic, and at rest for databases, disks and backups holding sensitive data
End-to-end for data the operator should never see, such as private messages
Field-level encryption for especially sensitive values such as card or health data
whenNotToUse: As a substitute for access control, since a compromised app with the key can still read everything
Inventing your own algorithm or protocol: use vetted libraries and defaults
pitfalls: Storing the encryption key next to the encrypted data
Reusing a nonce with the same key, or using an unauthenticated mode such as plain CBC or ECB
Assuming 'encrypted at rest' protects against an attacker who has compromised the running server
Never testing key rotation or restore, so recovery fails when it matters

roles.label: User
roles.description: Owns the data and may hold a key.

roles.label: Application
roles.description: Encrypts and decrypts, using keys it can reach.

roles.label: Storage
roles.description: Holds ciphertext on disk or in a database.

quiz.question: A team turns on full-disk encryption for its database servers. Later, a SQL injection bug lets an attacker dump the notes table through the application. How much did the disk encryption help?
options: It helped fully, because every row on disk is ciphertext, so the dump is unreadable.
It helped partly, as long as the AES key is rotated every day and kept in a hardware security module.
No, because the live database decrypts for any query the app makes. It protects stolen disks.
It helped, because injection bugs cannot read encrypted volumes at all.
quiz.explanation: Encryption at rest protects data when the storage is taken away. A query that runs through the live application sees plaintext, as the app does. Rotation does not change that.

quiz.question: A service encrypts files before storing them in a bucket. The AES key sits in a config file in the same bucket. The team must keep data safe if the bucket leaks. What is the best design?
options: Use a key management service for the master key and wrap per-file data keys.
Encode the key file with base64 and give it an unrelated name.
Encrypt the key with a second key kept in the same bucket.
Move the config file to another folder of the bucket with stricter permissions.
quiz.explanation: Envelope encryption keeps the key that matters in a separate, access-controlled system, so a leaked bucket holds only ciphertext and wrapped keys. The other options leave every secret that is needed within reach of whoever gets the bucket.

quiz.question: To let the database find equal values, a developer encrypts every record with AES-GCM using the same key and one fixed 12-byte nonce, so equal inputs give equal outputs. What is the most serious problem?
options: It only reveals which records are identical, since the key stays secret.
It breaks secrecy and integrity: ciphertexts expose relations, and tags can be forged.
It is safe for data under a few gigabytes, since nonce reuse matters only at large volumes.
It slows encryption down, because GCM has to recompute its tables for a repeated nonce.
quiz.explanation: Reusing a nonce under one key lets an attacker combine ciphertexts to learn about the plaintexts, and it exposes the value used for authentication tags. Leaking equality is only the mild part. Use a unique nonce, or a separate keyed hash for lookups.
